books.section: Watergate, the Undoing of President Nixon, and the Limits of Presidential Power

source: original; stimulus table compiled from the list of presidents in the grounding books

stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from the list of presidents in the grounding books (Barron's Ch. 10 timeline; 5 Steps Chs. 25-28; Princeton Ch. 12).
stimulus.text:
Presidents of the United States, 1945-1980:

| President | Party | Years in office |
| Harry S. Truman | Democratic | 1945-1953 |
| Dwight D. Eisenhower | Republican | 1953-1961 |
| John F. Kennedy | Democratic | 1961-1963 |
| Lyndon B. Johnson | Democratic | 1963-1969 |
| Richard Nixon | Republican | 1969-1974 |
| Gerald Ford | Republican | 1974-1977 |
| Jimmy Carter | Democratic | 1977-1981 |

stem: What does the pattern of parties in the table best show about presidential politics from 1945 to 1980?

options.text: One party controlled the White House without interruption for the whole period from 1945 to 1980.
options.misconception: The table switches parties four times between 1945 and 1981.

options.text: Voters never returned a sitting president to office, so each president served only a single term in the White House.
options.misconception: Eisenhower served from 1953 to 1961, eight years, so voters did return a sitting president.

options.text: Control of the White House changed hands regularly, with neither party holding it more than eight straight years.
Presidential elections stopped mattering because the same few men stayed in office year after year without any change.
options.misconception: The table names seven different presidents, so the office kept changing hands.

rationales.A: The table switches parties four times between 1945 and 1981.
rationales.B: Eisenhower served from 1953 to 1961, eight years, so voters did return a sitting president.
rationales.C: The table changes parties in 1953, 1961, 1969, and 1977, and the longest run by one party is eight years.
rationales.D: The table names seven different presidents, so the office kept changing hands.
rationales.general:
1. Walk down the Party column: Democrat, Republican, Democrat, Democrat, Republican, Republican, Democrat.
2. The party changes in 1953, 1961, 1969, and 1977, so no party held the office for the whole period.
3. Count the longest run: eight years, from 1945 to 1953, from 1953 to 1961, and from 1961 to 1969.
4. Background: The regular switching fits a competitive two-party system, not one-party rule.
Remember: To judge a pattern, count the runs in the table instead of remembering one election.
